lessons.title: The Skeletal System: Bones and Functions
lessons.description: Major bones of the skeleton, the six functions of the skeleton and how the skeletal system supports physical activity.
lessons.content_html:
The Framework of Movement

The human skeleton is a living structure made of 206 bones that provides the framework for every movement you make in sport. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against. The skeleton works in partnership with the muscular system: muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints. Understanding which bones are where — and what they do — underpins everything else in PE.

Bones of the Skeleton: Head to Toe

Working from the top of the body downwards, the cranium sits at the very top of the head, curving down around the brain. Below it, the vertebrae form a column of 33 bones running from the base of the skull to the pelvis — protecting the spinal cord and giving the trunk both stability and a controlled range of movement. At the front of the chest, the sternum (breastbone) and the ribs form the ribcage, encasing the heart and lungs. The clavicle (collarbone) connects the sternum to the shoulder on each side, and the flat, triangular scapula (shoulder blade) lies across the upper back.

The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Together, the scapula and humerus form the shoulder joint — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the body. At the elbow, three bones meet: the humerus, the radius (which runs along the thumb side of the forearm) and the ulna (which runs along the little-finger side). In the wrist and hand, the carpals form the wrist, the metacarpals form the palm, and the phalanges are the finger bones. These hand bones are named explicitly in the OCR specification and are examined directly — learn all three.

Moving to the lower body, the pelvis is a large basin-shaped structure at the base of the spine. It forms the hip joint with the head of the femur — a ball-and-socket joint allowing the greatest range of movement in the lower limb. At the knee, the femur articulates with the tibia (the large shin bone), forming a hinge joint. The patella sits in front of the knee joint. The fibula runs alongside the tibia on the outer side of the lower leg. At the foot, the tarsals form the ankle and heel, the metatarsals form the arch of the foot, and the phalanges are the toe bones — mirroring the hand structure.

Key Fact

OCR’s 19 named bones: cranium, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, clavicle, scapula, pelvis, humerus, ulna, radius, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals. The hand and foot bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, tarsals, metatarsals) are OCR-specific additions — make sure you can name and locate all of them.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton does far more than hold the body upright. It serves six distinct functions, each of which can be applied directly to sport and physical activity.

Support — the skeleton holds the body upright against gravity. A sprinter’s lower limbs support their entire body weight as they drive off the blocks. Without a rigid skeletal frame, the muscular system would have nothing to act on.

Posture — the vertebral column and pelvis maintain the upright alignment of the body. Good posture keeps the skeleton in correct mechanical alignment, reducing injury risk and allowing muscles to work most efficiently. A rower must maintain an upright spine throughout the drive phase; poor posture transfers force inefficiently and risks back injury. OCR lists posture as a distinct function, separate from support — always treat them as two separate marks.

Protection — flat bones protect vital organs. The cranium shields the brain; the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs. In contact sports such as rugby, the ribcage absorbs impact forces that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs directly.

Movement — bones act as levers. When the biceps contracts during a bicep curl, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) pivot at the elbow to lift the load. In kicking a football, the femur swings at the hip and the tibia swings at the knee, producing explosive leg extension.

Blood cell production — red bone marrow inside flat and irregular bones produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles during exercise via haemoglobin. This function links directly to cardiovascular performance: a well-functioning skeletal system supports oxygen delivery to muscles.

Storage of minerals — bones store calcium and phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when the body needs them, and weight-bearing exercise stimulates the bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production and storage of minerals. Each one links to sporting performance — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement), the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection), and the vertebral column maintains alignment during a rowing drive (posture).

A very common error is to list only five functions and miss posture entirely, or to treat posture and support as the same thing. In OCR, they are explicitly two separate functions. Support is about bearing the weight of the body against gravity — the skeleton stops you collapsing. Posture is about maintaining correct alignment and shape during movement — the spine and pelvis keep the body in the optimal mechanical position for efficient performance and injury prevention. In an exam, if you write “support/posture” as one combined answer, you will likely receive credit for only one function. Always list them separately and give a different sporting example for each.

OCR explicitly requires students to name and locate the carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), tarsals and metatarsals in addition to the major long bones. These bones matter in sport: the carpals and metacarpals absorb force during a gymnast’s handstand or a goalkeeper’s diving save; the metatarsals and tarsals form the arch of the foot, which distributes body weight during running and jumping. A question asking “name the bones of the hand” expects all three groups: carpals (wrist), metacarpals (palm) and phalanges (fingers).
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about skeletal functions, name a function, explain what it means, and apply it to a sport — that’s the three marks. On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question, avoid listing functions as bullet points. Instead, write in continuous prose: state the function, explain how it works, and link it to a named sporting movement. OCR’s key difference from other boards is the inclusion of posture as a separate, sixth function — always list it separately from support and use a different sport example. If asked to name bones at a joint, state both (or all three) bones: the knee joint involves the femur and tibia; the elbow involves the humerus, radius and ulna. Failing to name all articulating bones costs marks on identify-the-bones questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR requires 19 named bones, including the hand bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) and foot bones (tarsals, metatarsals) in addition to the major long bones — learn all 19 and their locations.
  • The six functions of the skeleton are support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production and storage of minerals — OCR lists posture as a distinct function, so always treat it separately from support in exam answers.
  • Each function can be linked directly to sporting performance: levers for movement, ribcage for protection in contact sport, bone marrow producing red blood cells that carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic exercise.

lessons.title: Synovial Joints and Movement at Joints
lessons.description: Hinge and ball-and-socket joints, articulating bones and the types of movement they allow.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Synovial Joint?

Every freely movable joint in the body — at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee — is a synovial joint. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body, and they all share the same basic structure: a capsule surrounding the joint, fluid inside to reduce friction, and a range of soft-tissue structures that hold the joint together and prevent injury. Understanding these structures is important not just for anatomy, but for explaining how joints withstand the demands of sport.

Structures of a Synovial Joint

The outer shell of a synovial joint is the joint capsule. It is made of tough, fibrous connective tissue that wraps completely around the joint, holding the bones in position and containing the joint fluid. Inside the capsule, the synovial membrane lines the inner surface and produces synovial fluid — a viscous substance that coats the ends of the bones inside the joint, dramatically reducing friction and allowing bones to glide smoothly past each other. During the warm-up phase of exercise, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and spreads more effectively, which is one reason why warming up reduces injury risk.

Covering the ends of the bones inside the joint is articular cartilage, a smooth tissue that absorbs compressive forces and provides an almost frictionless surface. Ligaments are short, tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect bone to bone across the joint — the primary restraints against excessive movement. Tendons connect muscles to bone, transmitting contractile force to the skeleton to produce movement at the joint.

Key Fact

The four key components of a synovial joint: synovial fluid (lubricates and reduces friction between bone surfaces), articular cartilage (absorbs compression, provides frictionless surface), ligaments (connect bone to bone, prevent excessive movement), tendons (connect muscle to bone, transmit force for movement).

Types of Synovial Joint

OCR identifies two types of synovial joint and four specific joints that are directly examined. A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only — flexion and extension. The knee (femur articulating with the tibia) and the elbow (humerus articulating with the radius and ulna) are both hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in multiple planes. The shoulder (head of the humerus fitting into the socket of the scapula) and the hip (head of the femur fitting into the socket of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints.

Articulating Bones at Each Joint

The OCR specification requires you to name the articulating bones at all four joints. At the knee, the femur (thigh bone) articulates with the tibia (shin bone) — these two long bones form the hinge. At the elbow, the humerus articulates with both the radius and the ulna — three bones meet here, which is why the elbow allows both hinge movement (flexion/extension) and some rotation. At the shoulder, the humerus articulates with the scapula — the rounded head of the humerus sits in the shallow socket of the scapula, enabling the greatest range of movement in the body. At the hip, the femur articulates with the pelvis — the rounded head of the femur slots into the deep cup of the pelvis, creating a stable but mobile ball-and-socket joint.

Key Fact

Knee: femur + tibia (hinge). Elbow: humerus + radius + ulna (hinge). Shoulder: humerus + scapula (ball-and-socket). Hip: femur + pelvis (ball-and-socket). These are the four joints on the OCR specification — learn the articulating bones for each.

Types of Movement at Joints

Flexion is a decrease in the angle at a joint — bending. Extension is an increase in the angle — straightening. Both occur at all four OCR joints. At the elbow and knee (hinge joints), flexion and extension are the only movements possible because the structure of the joint restricts movement to a single plane.

At the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket joints), a much wider range of movements is available. Abduction is movement of a limb away from the midline — lifting the arm out to the side in a star jump. Adduction is movement towards the midline — bringing the arm back down. Both abduction and adduction are available at the shoulder and hip but not at the elbow or knee.

Rotation of the shoulder is turning the arm in or out along its long axis. A cricket bowler’s arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery. Circumduction of the shoulder is a circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the arm traces a full cone shape. Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.

A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); articular cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.

As body temperature rises during a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and distributes more evenly across the joint surfaces. This increases the range of movement available and reduces friction, meaning joints can work more efficiently. Ligaments and tendons also become more pliable at higher temperatures, reducing the risk of tears. This is the physiological reason why a warm-up includes a pulse raiser and stretching before high-intensity work.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a ‘State Two’ question about synovial joint structures, give two genuinely different structures — do not write two answers that describe the same component. Spread your answers: one structural component (e.g. ligaments) and one lubricating component (e.g. synovial fluid) will demonstrate wider knowledge. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question about movement types, state the movement, define it (angle increasing/decreasing, towards/away from midline), name the joint where it occurs, and give a sporting example — that covers all four marks. When naming articulating bones, state all the bones at a joint: the elbow has three articulating bones (humerus, radius and ulna) — writing only two loses a mark. OCR does not require plantar flexion or dorsiflexion in this section — the four named joints and their standard movement types are the focus.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Synovial joints share four key components: synovial fluid (reduces friction), articular cartilage (absorbs compression), ligaments (bone to bone, prevent excessive movement) and tendons (muscle to bone, transmit force) — each can be linked to injury prevention in sport.
  • The four OCR joints with their articulating bones: knee (femur + tibia, hinge), elbow (humerus + radius + ulna, hinge), shoulder (humerus + scapula, ball-and-socket), hip (femur + pelvis, ball-and-socket).
  • Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder and hip) allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction. Hinge joints (elbow, knee) allow flexion and extension only.

lessons.title: Muscles and Antagonistic Pairs
lessons.description: Major muscle groups, agonist, antagonist and fixator roles in antagonistic muscle action.
lessons.content_html:
Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. OCR also requires knowledge of a third muscle role — the fixator — which stabilises a nearby joint while movement occurs at another.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The trapezius is the large, diamond-shaped muscle that runs from the base of the skull down to the middle of the back. It elevates the shoulders, pulls the scapula back and assists head movement. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the broad muscle of the lower and mid-back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder — powerful in swimming backstroke and rowing movements. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the press-up or front crawl pull phase.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting and shortening to pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder throughout the bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow moves.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser and fixator.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping.

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping.

Key Fact

In the upward phase of a bicep curl: biceps = agonist (prime mover, contracts to flex the elbow), triceps = antagonist (relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), deltoid = fixator (stabilises the shoulder joint so the upper arm stays still). In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist.

Key Fact

The human body contains over 600 named muscles. Muscle fibres are packed with mitochondria — the organelles that produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying the energy needed for sustained muscular contraction during sport and exercise.

OCR explicitly requires three muscle roles — agonist, antagonist and fixator — while other boards only require two. Students who name only the agonist and antagonist will miss the fixator marks in OCR questions. A fixator is a muscle that holds a nearby body part still so that the prime mover can work efficiently. It does not produce the movement; it provides the stable base from which the movement occurs. In the bicep curl, the deltoid stabilises the shoulder joint throughout the exercise — without it, the shoulder would move and the elbow flexion would be inefficient. Always include the fixator and name the joint it stabilises.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist and fixator. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), fixator named and its role described (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.”
lessons.exam_tip_html: For any OCR question asking about muscle roles during a movement, you must include all three roles: agonist (which muscle produces the movement), antagonist (which muscle relaxes to allow the movement), and fixator (which muscle stabilises the nearby joint). Missing the fixator is the most common reason students lose marks on this topic. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question, the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for the agonist, 1 for the antagonist, 1 for the fixator with its joint, and 1 for accurately describing what each does in that specific movement. A common error is to say the antagonist ‘contracts’ — the antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement to occur. Make sure your sporting example specifies the phase of movement (e.g. ‘during the upward phase of a bicep curl’) to make it clear which muscle is the agonist at that moment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR requires three muscle roles: the agonist (prime mover that contracts to produce movement), the antagonist (which relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), and the fixator (which stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover can work efficiently). Always name all three in exam answers.
  • Key sporting pairs: biceps/triceps at the elbow (deltoid fixator), quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee, gluteals/hip flexors at the hip, gastrocnemius as prime mover for plantar flexion.
  • OCR’s extended muscle list includes deltoid, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, pectorals, biceps, triceps, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals and gastrocnemius — know the location and primary action of each.

lessons.title: Lever Systems in Sport
lessons.description: First, second and third class levers in the body and the meaning of mechanical advantage.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Lever System?

The human body is a machine built from levers. Every time you nod your head, rise onto your toes, or perform a bicep curl, you are using a lever system to transmit force. Understanding how levers work allows coaches and athletes to explain why some movements generate great force, and why others allow great speed but require more effort. A lever consists of three components arranged around a pivot point. The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point — in the body, a joint. The load (also called the resistance) is the weight or force being moved. The effort is the force applied to move that load — in the body, this is the force produced by the contracting muscle. The three classes of lever differ in the relative positions of these three components: fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E).

Key Fact

OCR pins each lever class to a specific body location: 1st class = neck (nodding the head), 2nd class = ankle (calf raise / plantar flexion), 3rd class = elbow (bicep curl). Learn these three locations — they are the examples OCR examines directly.

First Class Levers

In a first class lever, the fulcrum sits between the load and the effort. Think of a seesaw: the pivot is in the middle, with weight on one side and the pushing force on the other. In the body, the OCR example is the nodding action of the head at the neck: the skull (load) rests at one end, the neck extensor muscles (effort) pull from behind, and the atlantooccipital joint (fulcrum) sits between them. First class levers can produce both force and speed depending on where the effort and load arms fall relative to the fulcrum.

Second Class Levers

In a second class lever, the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. The classic everyday example is a wheelbarrow. In the body, the OCR example is plantar flexion at the ankle — rising onto the toes (a calf raise): the ball of the foot acts as the fulcrum at one end, the body weight (load) acts through the ankle joint in the middle, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (effort) pull via the Achilles tendon at the heel. The effort arm is longer than the load arm, so a relatively small muscular effort can move a larger load. Second class levers therefore produce a mechanical advantage greater than 1, making them excellent for force production.

Third Class Levers

In a third class lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. This is the most common lever arrangement in the human body. The OCR example is elbow flexion during a bicep curl: the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps apply effort just below the joint, and the load (the forearm, hand and any weight held) is at the far end. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so more muscular effort is needed to move the load. However, a small movement of the biceps produces a large movement of the hand — trading mechanical disadvantage for speed and range of movement. Third class levers therefore favour speed and range over force, which is why most striking and throwing actions in sport use them.

A very common exam error is mis-labelling the positions of the fulcrum, load and effort, or confusing which class a sporting example belongs to. A reliable approach is to identify the joint first (that is always the fulcrum), then identify what is being moved (the load, usually the body part or any weight), and finally identify where the muscle pulls (the effort). Once you have these three pinned, the class follows logically: if the joint (F) is in the middle, it is first class; if the weight (L) is in the middle, it is second class; if the muscle pull (E) is in the middle, it is third class. Anchor your answer to OCR’s three named body locations: neck (1st), ankle (2nd), elbow (3rd).

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage is a number that tells you whether a lever amplifies force or amplifies speed and range of movement. It compares the length of the effort arm (the distance from the fulcrum to where the effort is applied) with the length of the load arm (the distance from the fulcrum to where the load acts).

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the effort arm is longer than the load arm — a small effort produces a large force. This is the case in second class levers: rising onto the toes lifts your entire body weight with relatively modest calf muscle effort. A mechanical advantage less than 1 means the load arm is longer than the effort arm — more muscular effort is required, but the trade-off is greater speed and range. Third class levers have MA less than 1 — that is why bicep curls, throwing and striking actions require significant muscular effort but produce fast, wide movements at the end of the limb.

Unlike some other exam boards, OCR only requires you to know the definition of mechanical advantage — not to calculate it. You need to be able to explain what mechanical advantage means and state whether a given lever has an advantage greater than or less than 1. A good exam answer on mechanical advantage will: (1) state whether the effort arm or load arm is longer, (2) say whether this gives a MA greater than or less than 1, and (3) explain what that means for force production or speed. For example: “At the ankle during a calf raise, the effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) is longer than the load arm (heel to ankle joint), so the lever has a mechanical advantage greater than 1, meaning the calf muscles produce more force than the load they are lifting.”

Key Fact

Mechanical advantage greater than 1 = force is amplified (second class lever, e.g. ankle during a calf raise). Mechanical advantage less than 1 = speed and range of movement are amplified (most third class levers, e.g. elbow during a bicep curl). First class levers can have MA either above or below 1 depending on the relative positions of the fulcrum, load and effort.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a ‘Describe’ question asking you to describe a lever system in a sporting example, always name all three components (fulcrum, load and effort) and identify which body part acts as each. The fulcrum is always the joint — a common error is labelling the muscle itself as the fulcrum. On the 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ question about lever systems, make sure you evaluate both sides: what advantages does a particular lever system bring to performance, and what are its limitations? For example, third class levers (elbow in a throw) allow great speed but require significant muscular effort. A balanced answer anchors each point to a named sporting action. OCR only requires the definition of mechanical advantage, not a calculation — express it as “greater than 1” or “less than 1” and explain what that means for force or speed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR’s three lever class body locations: 1st class = neck (head nodding), 2nd class = ankle (calf raise / plantar flexion), 3rd class = elbow (bicep curl). Always anchor your examples to these named locations.
  • Mechanical advantage greater than 1 favours force production (second class lever); mechanical advantage less than 1 favours speed and range of movement (most third class levers). OCR requires the definition only, not a calculation.
  • In any exam question on levers, identify the joint (fulcrum), what is being moved (load) and where the muscle pulls (effort) before classifying the lever. Getting these three positions right is the key to avoiding the most common exam error.

lessons.title: Planes and Axes of Movement
lessons.description: Frontal, transverse and sagittal planes and frontal, transverse and longitudinal axes in sporting actions.
lessons.content_html:
Imagining the Body in Three Dimensions

When a gymnast performs a forward roll, a discus thrower spins in a full circle, or a dancer executes a cartwheel, their body is moving through space in a precise, describable way. Movement analysts use a system of planes and axes to describe exactly which direction that movement occurs and around which line the body rotates. Mastering this system is essential for analysing sport performance.

Imagine the body standing upright in the anatomical position — feet together, palms facing forwards. Now picture three flat sheets of glass slicing through the body, each at right angles to the others. These are the three planes of movement. For every plane there is a matching axis: a rod passing through the body at right angles to that plane, forming the pivot point for rotation in that plane.

Key Fact

OCR’s three planes and their matching axes: sagittal plane → transverse axis; frontal plane → frontal axis; transverse plane → longitudinal axis. Note that OCR names the axis for the frontal plane as the frontal axis (not the sagittal axis used by some other boards). Learn the OCR terms precisely.

The Sagittal Plane and Transverse Axis

The sagittal plane runs from front to back, dividing the body into a left half and a right half. Movement in this plane involves the body moving forwards or backwards. The matching axis is the transverse axis, which runs from side to side like a rod passing through both hips.

Classic sporting actions in the sagittal plane include a forward somersault (gymnastics or trampolining) and a forward roll. In both cases the body rotates in a forwards direction around the transverse axis. Running also takes place primarily in the sagittal plane, as the arms and legs swing forwards and backwards. A back somersault is also in the sagittal plane, but the rotation is in the opposite direction around the same transverse axis.

A common misconception is that any large movement must involve multiple planes. In running, the limbs swing forward and backward — that is purely sagittal-plane motion. A cartwheel, however, takes the body to the side rather than forward: the legs move apart and the body tips sideways, rotating around the frontal axis in the frontal plane. The key question is always: “Which direction does the body travel, and around which axis does it rotate?” Always answer both before identifying the plane and axis.

The Frontal Plane and Frontal Axis

The frontal plane runs from side to side, dividing the body into a front half and a back half. Movements in this plane take the body out to the side or bring it back in. The matching axis is the frontal axis, which runs from front to back like a rod passing through the navel and the spine.

The cartwheel is the clearest sporting example of the frontal plane. The gymnast tips their entire body sideways over their hands, rotating around the frontal axis. Abduction and adduction movements at the shoulder and hip also occur in the frontal plane — for instance, a star jump sees the arms and legs moving away from and back to the midline of the body in the frontal plane around the frontal axis.

The Transverse Plane and Longitudinal Axis

The transverse plane runs horizontally, dividing the body into an upper half and a lower half. Think of it as a table top cutting through the body at waist height. Movements in this plane involve twisting or spinning. The matching axis is the longitudinal axis, which runs from the top of the head straight down through the spine to the feet.

Sporting examples of transverse-plane movement around the longitudinal axis include a 360° twist in ice skating, a discus thrower rotating in a circle before release, and a figure skater pulling in their arms to spin faster. In all of these, the performer is rotating horizontally around a vertical axis running through the middle of their body.

Key Fact

The three OCR sporting triplets: forward somersault → sagittal plane, transverse axis. Cartwheel → frontal plane, frontal axis. 360° spin / ice spin → transverse plane, longitudinal axis. Commit these to memory as a set — exam questions ask you to identify both the plane and the axis.

Applying Planes and Axes to Joint Movements

The plane-and-axis framework also maps directly onto the joint movements covered in the musculoskeletal system. Flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane around the transverse axis. Abduction and adduction occur in the frontal plane around the frontal axis. Rotation at the shoulder or hip occurs in the transverse plane around the longitudinal axis. This connection means that when you analyse a sporting action, you can describe both the joint movement and the plane and axis in which it occurs, giving a much richer technical account.

A very important distinction: OCR names the axis associated with the frontal plane as the frontal axis. Some other boards call this the “sagittal axis.” If you have studied another board’s materials, you must use OCR’s terminology in your exam answers or risk losing marks. The three OCR axes are: transverse axis (for the sagittal plane), frontal axis (for the frontal plane), and longitudinal axis (for the transverse plane). Never write “sagittal axis” in an OCR answer — this is not a term OCR uses for axes of rotation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on planes and axes typically ask you to identify both the plane and axis for a named sporting action — always give both. A common error is naming only the plane without the axis. Remember OCR’s three triplets: forward somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, frontal axis), 360° spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis). Critically, OCR uses “frontal axis” for the axis of the frontal plane — not “sagittal axis.” Writing “sagittal axis” on an OCR paper will cost marks. On ‘explain’ questions, add one sentence describing the direction of rotation: “A forward somersault occurs in the sagittal plane because the body rotates forwards and backwards around the transverse axis, which runs from side to side through the hips.” For extended-response questions, connect the plane-and-axis description to the joint action (flexion, abduction) and the muscles involved.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three planes divide the body into halves — sagittal (left/right), frontal (front/back) and transverse (upper/lower) — and each has a matching axis at right angles to it: transverse axis, frontal axis and longitudinal axis respectively.
  • The three OCR triplets to memorise: forward somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, frontal axis) and 360° ice spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis).
  • OCR uses “frontal axis” (not sagittal axis) for rotations in the frontal plane. Joint movements map to planes: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, abduction/adduction in the frontal plane, rotation in the transverse plane.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System and Pathway of Blood
lessons.description: Heart structure, pulmonary and systemic circulation, blood vessels and key cardiac definitions.
lessons.content_html:
The Double-Circulatory System

The cardiovascular system uses a double-circulatory system. This means blood makes two separate loops before returning to its starting point. The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is collected, before returning the now-oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart. The systemic circulation then carries that oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart out to every organ and muscle in the body, returning deoxygenated blood to the right side of the heart via the veins. Separating these two loops prevents oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood from mixing, ensuring maximum efficiency of oxygen delivery to the working muscles.

The Heart: Structure and Function

The heart is a hollow, muscular organ roughly the size of a fist, located in the chest slightly left of centre behind the sternum. It is divided into four chambers by a central wall called the septum. The two upper chambers are called atria (singular: atrium) — the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body, and the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. The two lower chambers are called ventricles — the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. The left ventricle has a thicker, more muscular wall than the right because it must generate much higher pressure to push blood all the way around the body.

Valves inside the heart prevent the backflow of blood. The bicuspid valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle. The semilunar valves are located at the exit of each ventricle, where the aorta leaves the left ventricle and where the pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle. All three sets of valves open due to changes in blood pressure and close automatically to maintain one-directional blood flow.

Key Fact

Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs (gas exchange) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → semilunar valve → aorta → body. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the opposite of most arteries.

The Pathway of Blood Through the Heart

Following the pathway of blood precisely is a common exam demand. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava. From the right atrium it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle contracts and forces blood through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is picked up by haemoglobin in the red blood cells. The now-oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the pulmonary vein, entering the left atrium. It passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, which contracts powerfully, ejecting oxygenated blood through the semilunar valve into the aorta — from which it is distributed to every organ and muscle in the body.

The Role of Red Blood Cells

Red blood cells are the oxygen-carrying cells of the blood. They contain haemoglobin — a red iron-containing protein that binds readily with oxygen in the oxygen-rich environment of the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin. When red blood cells reach the working muscles, where oxygen concentration is low, oxyhaemoglobin breaks down and releases its oxygen into the muscle tissue. The same red blood cells then pick up carbon dioxide — a waste product of respiration — and carry it back to the lungs to be exhaled. Without red blood cells in sufficient numbers, oxygen transport collapses and athletic performance is severely impaired.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular walls because they must withstand the high pressure generated by ventricular contraction. The walls are elastic, allowing them to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing out blood flow. All arteries (except the pulmonary artery) carry oxygenated blood.

Veins carry blood back towards the heart. They have thinner walls than arteries because blood pressure is much lower. Veins contain valves that prevent backflow, which is especially important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity. All veins (except the pulmonary vein) carry deoxygenated blood.

Capillaries are the microscopic vessels that form the link between arteries and veins in the tissues. Their walls are just one cell thick, allowing oxygen and nutrients to diffuse into the muscle cells and carbon dioxide and waste products to diffuse back into the blood. Every working muscle is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Long-term aerobic training increases capillary density in muscles, improving oxygen delivery.

One of the most common errors in cardiovascular questions is stating that the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood. It does not. The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood — it takes blood from the right ventricle to the lungs specifically so that oxygen can be collected. Similarly, the pulmonary vein is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood — returning fresh blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The rule “arteries carry oxygenated blood” has two exceptions that you must memorise: the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated away from heart) and the pulmonary vein (oxygenated toward heart).

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Three linked measurements describe how efficiently the heart pumps blood. Stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of the heart with each beat. At rest, stroke volume is approximately 70 ml. Heart rate is the number of beats per minute (bpm). A typical resting heart rate is 60–80 bpm (trained endurance athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 bpm — a long-term adaptation called bradycardia). Cardiac output (Q) is the product of the two:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

At rest: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min (approximately 5 litres per minute). During intense exercise, heart rate can rise to 200 bpm or more and stroke volume increases to around 110–130 ml, so cardiac output can reach 20–25 litres per minute in a trained athlete.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. Always show the formula, substitute the values, and include the unit (ml/min or L/min). Example: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min. At maximum exercise this can rise to over 20,000 ml/min in a trained athlete.

During exercise, the working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose than at rest. The body redistributes blood flow so that a greater proportion of cardiac output goes to the active muscles. Blood supply to the digestive system and other non-essential organs is reduced, while blood flow to the working skeletal muscles and heart muscle increases dramatically. This redistribution is an important short-term effect of exercise. It explains why exercising vigorously immediately after a large meal can cause discomfort — the digestive system is competing with the muscles for blood supply at a time when the muscles' demands are greatly elevated.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The cardiac output calculation is one of the most predictable questions in this topic — always worth attempting. Show three things: (1) the formula (Q = stroke volume × heart rate), (2) the substitution with figures from the question, and (3) the answer with the correct unit (ml/min or L/min). Missing the unit is a frequent error that costs the final mark. On a ‘Describe the pathway of blood’ question, a common mistake is to say the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood — it is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. OCR also requires you to name the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves and place them correctly in the blood pathway — not just state that “valves prevent backflow.” For the 8-mark Evaluate question, ensure your argument covers both sides: address what happens when the cardiovascular system functions efficiently and consider what happens when it is under stress, linking both to the specific sporting context given.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The cardiovascular system uses a double-circulatory system: pulmonary circulation (heart ↔ lungs) and systemic circulation (heart ↔ body). Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → semilunar valve → aorta → body.
  • Red blood cells carry oxygen (bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin) to the working muscles and transport carbon dioxide back to the lungs for removal.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (approximately 5 L/min at rest; up to 25 L/min during maximal exercise in a trained athlete). During exercise, blood flow is redistributed to the working muscles.

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
lessons.description: Pathway of air, the role of respiratory muscles and gas exchange at the alveoli.
lessons.content_html:
The Journey Air Takes Into Your Body

Every time you inhale, air travels along a precisely ordered pathway before oxygen reaches your working muscles. Understanding this route is essential for explaining how the body meets the increased demand for oxygen during exercise. Air enters through the mouth or nose, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered. It then passes into the trachea — the windpipe — which is kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. From the trachea, air divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), one entering each lung. Inside the lungs, the bronchi branch repeatedly into smaller and smaller tubes called bronchioles. The bronchioles finally open out into tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus), and it is here that the vital process of gas exchange occurs.

Key Fact

The pathway of air follows six stages in sequence: mouth/nose → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. OCR specifically includes both mouth and nose at the start of the pathway. Commit this order to memory — it appears regularly in short-answer questions.

Gaseous Exchange at the Alveoli

Gaseous exchange is the movement of gases between the lungs and the bloodstream. It relies on diffusion — molecules naturally move from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. In the alveoli, the concentration of oxygen is high (freshly inhaled air) while the blood arriving from the body has a low oxygen concentration and a high concentration of carbon dioxide. As a result, oxygen diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, out of the blood and into the alveolus to be exhaled.

Six structural features of the alveoli are specifically designed to maximise the speed and efficiency of this exchange. First, the alveoli have a very large surface area in total — hundreds of millions of tiny sacs create an enormous surface for diffusion to occur across. Second, the alveolar walls are moist and only one cell thick, meaning the distance gases must travel is as short as possible. Third, the alveoli are surrounded by a rich network of capillaries, ensuring a continuous and large blood supply. Fourth, blood flowing through these capillaries is constantly replenished (deoxygenated blood arrives and oxygenated blood leaves), which maintains the concentration gradient that drives diffusion.

Once oxygen crosses into the blood, it binds with haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. This oxygenated blood then travels via the pulmonary veins to the left side of the heart and is pumped out to the working muscles. Haemoglobin can also carry carbon dioxide on the return journey to the lungs.

A common misunderstanding is that oxygen delivery to muscles is purely about breathing harder. In fact, the rate of diffusion at the alveoli is limited by concentration gradients and surface area — you cannot increase the surface area of your alveoli by trying harder. What exercise does achieve is an increased breathing rate and deeper breaths (greater tidal volume), which refreshes the air in the alveoli more frequently, maintaining a strong concentration gradient. Additionally, more capillaries open up around active alveoli during exercise, increasing the effective surface area available for gas exchange. The structural adaptations of the alveoli — thin walls, large surface area, rich blood supply — are what make rapid exchange possible, not effort alone.

The Mechanics of Breathing

Breathing is an active mechanical process driven by muscles changing the volume and pressure inside the chest cavity. During inhalation at rest, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, while the intercostal muscles contract to raise the rib cage upward and outward. These combined actions increase the volume of the chest cavity, which lowers the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure. Air rushes in from outside to equalise the pressure — this is inhalation. During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax. The rib cage falls inward and downward under gravity, reducing the chest volume and increasing pressure in the lungs. Air is pushed out passively. Breathing at rest is therefore largely passive on the exhale.

During intense exercise, the body must move air much more forcefully and rapidly. On the inhale, accessory muscles come into play: the pectorals (chest muscles) help to elevate the rib cage further and faster. On the exhale, the abdominal muscles actively contract, pulling the rib cage down more quickly and forcefully expelling air. This ensures that stale air (rich in carbon dioxide) is cleared from the lungs faster, making room for fresh, oxygen-rich air.

Breathing Rate, Tidal Volume and Minute Ventilation

Breathing rate is the number of breaths taken per minute. At rest, a typical breathing rate is around 12–15 breaths per minute. During maximal exercise this can rise to 40–60 breaths per minute. Note that OCR uses the term “breathing rate” — not “respiratory rate.”

Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in or out with each breath. At rest, tidal volume is approximately 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise it can rise to 3 litres or more as the body draws on its deeper breath capacity.

Minute ventilation is the total volume of air moved per minute and equals tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate. For example, a resting athlete breathing at 15 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.5 litres has a minute ventilation of 7.5 litres per minute. During hard exercise, both tidal volume and breathing rate increase, so minute ventilation can rise to 100–150 litres per minute in trained performers. This enormous increase ensures the concentration gradient at the alveoli is maintained even as muscles consume oxygen at a high rate.

Key Fact

Six features make alveolar gas exchange efficient: large surface area, moist thin walls (one cell thick), short diffusion distance, large capillary network, large blood supply, and a maintained concentration gradient (high O2 in alveoli, low CO2 in arriving blood).

Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate. Always show the formula and include the unit (litres per minute or L/min). Example at rest: 0.5 L × 15 breaths/min = 7.5 L/min. Example during exercise: 2.5 L × 40 breaths/min = 100 L/min. A common error is using “respiratory rate” instead of “breathing rate” — OCR specifies breathing rate. Also make sure you do not confuse tidal volume (per breath) with minute ventilation (per minute).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “describe” questions on gaseous exchange, students often say oxygen “moves into the blood” without explaining why — the mark scheme almost always requires the word “diffusion” and a reference to the concentration gradient (high to low). For “state two” questions on respiratory muscles, do not give the same answer twice — naming both the diaphragm and intercostals is required; stating just “the breathing muscles” twice earns only one mark. For 6-mark “analyse” questions, go beyond description: link each structural feature of the alveolus to a specific sporting implication. For example, “the large surface area of the alveoli means a marathon runner can exchange sufficient oxygen even at race pace, sustaining aerobic energy production.” Bullet-point responses rarely score above the Developing band — extended-response questions reward connected prose where each point is developed with a sporting example. Always use the OCR term “breathing rate” not “respiratory rate.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Air travels in a fixed sequence — mouth/nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli — and gaseous exchange occurs at the alveoli by diffusion, driven by concentration gradients.
  • Six structural features of the alveoli (large surface area, thin moist walls, short diffusion pathway, rich capillary network, large blood supply, maintained concentration gradient) maximise the speed of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.
  • During exercise, tidal volume and breathing rate both increase, raising minute ventilation dramatically so the alveolar concentration gradient is maintained even under heavy muscular demand.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
lessons.description: Defining aerobic and anaerobic exercise and applying examples by intensity and duration.
lessons.content_html:
Two Ways Your Body Produces Energy

All physical activity requires energy, and the body produces that energy by breaking down glucose. The critical difference between the two energy pathways is whether sufficient oxygen is available. Aerobic exercise occurs when there is enough oxygen to fully break down glucose. The chemical summary is: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. This process is efficient, releasing large amounts of energy, and can be sustained for a long time — making it the dominant pathway for moderate-intensity, longer-duration activities such as a 10 km run, a long swim or a cycling time trial.

Anaerobic exercise occurs when the intensity of effort is so high that the cardiovascular system cannot deliver oxygen to the muscles fast enough. The body bypasses oxygen entirely and breaks down glucose without it: glucose → energy + lactic acid. This pathway is fast but inefficient — it produces far less energy per glucose molecule and cannot be sustained for long because lactic acid accumulates in the muscles, causing fatigue and the familiar burning sensation. Sprinting 100 m, an explosive plyometric jump or a short all-out rowing effort are classic examples of anaerobic activity.

Key Fact

Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. Anaerobic: glucose → energy + lactic acid. The key distinction is the presence or absence of sufficient oxygen — not simply whether the sport involves running or swimming.

Identifying Aerobic and Anaerobic Activity: Duration and Intensity

A common error is simply labelling a sport as “aerobic” or “anaerobic” without justifying the classification. The correct approach is to consider both the duration and the intensity of the effort. High-intensity activity lasting fewer than roughly ten seconds is almost entirely anaerobic because the demand for energy outpaces oxygen delivery. Activities lasting several minutes at moderate intensity are primarily aerobic. Many sports — such as football, netball and rugby — involve both pathways at different moments: a striker’s burst of speed to latch onto a through ball is anaerobic, but the sustained movement across the pitch throughout the match is predominantly aerobic.

Students often believe “aerobic” simply means easy or low-intensity exercise. This is incorrect. A trained 5,000 m runner racing at full competitive pace is still working aerobically — the intensity is high, but oxygen delivery keeps pace with demand throughout the race (approximately 13 minutes in duration). The correct justification is always intensity-and-duration together: “This activity is aerobic because the intensity, although high, can be maintained with sufficient oxygen delivery over the multi-minute duration.” Similarly, a short, explosive effort is anaerobic because the intensity is so extreme that oxygen cannot be delivered quickly enough — not because the activity is “hard” in some vague sense. Always frame your answer with both criteria.

Lactic Acid: Cause and Consequence

Lactic acid is produced whenever anaerobic respiration takes place — that is, whenever exercise intensity rises to the point where oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough. As lactic acid accumulates in the muscle fibres and bloodstream, it interferes with the chemical processes of muscle contraction and the athlete experiences the characteristic burning sensation and muscular fatigue. This is why anaerobic efforts cannot be sustained: a 100 m sprinter running at maximum effort will notice the burning onset in their legs in the final 20–30 metres of the race, and performance suffers unless the athlete eases off.

In many sports, the ability to tolerate or delay lactic acid accumulation is a key determinant of performance. A 400 m runner, for example, runs at an intensity that is predominantly anaerobic for approximately 45–50 seconds. Managing lactic acid accumulation through training — specifically by repeatedly stressing the anaerobic system in intervals — is a central goal of sprint conditioning programmes.

Many team sports require athletes to switch between aerobic and anaerobic energy systems within the same performance. In a game of basketball, a player spends much of the match jogging and walking (aerobic), but executes repeated explosive sprints, jumps and changes of direction (anaerobic). The same applies to a hockey winger or a rugby union flanker. When asked to classify the dominant energy system for a sport like this, consider what the athlete spends the most time doing, and what the critical performance moments demand. A basketball player’s overall fitness is predominantly aerobic; their game-deciding moments are predominantly anaerobic. Both systems must be trained.

Key Fact

Always justify aerobic/anaerobic classification using both intensity and duration. Aerobic examples: marathon running (moderate-high intensity, 2+ hours), 1,500 m swim (sustained effort over several minutes). Anaerobic examples: 100 m sprint (maximal intensity, ~10 seconds), shot-put throw (single explosive effort, under 3 seconds).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “identify” and shorter questions on aerobic vs anaerobic, a common error is giving the activity name without any justification. Even a 1-mark question may expect you to say why: “anaerobic, because the high intensity means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, students often produce one-sided answers that only describe the positive features of aerobic exercise without considering trade-offs, or vice versa. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Build your response using a “For X… However Y…” structure, anchor each point to a named sport or athlete type, and end with a justified conclusion. Also note: OCR does not require you to define or use the terms EPOC, oxygen debt or DOMS at this level — focus on the definitions, word equations and the intensity-duration justification.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Aerobic exercise uses oxygen to break down glucose fully (producing CO2 and water); anaerobic exercise occurs without sufficient oxygen and produces lactic acid as a by-product. Justify each classification with both intensity and duration evidence.
  • Lactic acid accumulates during anaerobic exercise, causing fatigue and the burning sensation in muscles. Activities lasting under approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity are predominantly anaerobic; sustained moderate-to-high intensity effort is predominantly aerobic.
  • Many sports use both systems: explosive moments (anaerobic) sit alongside sustained movement (aerobic). A complete athlete trains both energy pathways.

lessons.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
lessons.description: Immediate physiological responses and the long-term training adaptations of the body systems.
lessons.content_html:
Two Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across two distinct timescales in OCR’s specification, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Short-term effects occur during the exercise session itself and in the hours immediately after it — they are temporary and reverse once the body has recovered. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation — the body has permanently restructured itself to cope more efficiently with the demands of regular exercise. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Short-Term Effects: What Happens During and Immediately After Exercise

As exercise begins, several changes are immediately measurable. Muscle temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, increasing the speed of metabolic reactions and making the muscle tissue more pliable. Heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output all increase, responding to the greater demand for oxygen-carrying blood in the working muscles. Heart rate may climb from around 70 bpm at rest to 180 bpm or more during maximal effort, while stroke volume rises as the ventricles fill more completely and contract more forcefully.

A particularly important short-term effect for OCR is the redistribution of blood flow during exercise. The body redirects a greater proportion of cardiac output to the working skeletal muscles and the heart muscle itself, while blood supply to the digestive system and other non-essential organs is reduced. This ensures the muscles receive the oxygen and glucose they need during activity. Breathing rate and tidal volume both increase, raising minute ventilation to supply more oxygen to the lungs and remove carbon dioxide more rapidly. Oxygen delivery to the working muscles increases accordingly, supporting aerobic energy production. Where exercise intensity rises beyond the aerobic threshold, lactic acid production accelerates as the body supplements aerobic energy production with anaerobic pathways.

Key Fact

OCR’s six short-term effects of exercise: (1) increased muscle temperature; (2) increased heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output; (3) redistribution of blood flow during exercise; (4) increased breathing rate, tidal volume and minute ventilation; (5) increased oxygen delivery to the working muscles; (6) increased lactic acid production. All of these reverse when exercise stops.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations across multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it. OCR’s specification names a broader set of long-term adaptations than many other boards — all named adaptations below must be known precisely.

Muscular and Skeletal Adaptations

Regular resistance training produces hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles — the muscle fibres grow larger, producing greater strength and power. Muscular endurance improves as the muscles become better at sustaining repeated contractions without fatiguing. Closely linked is improved resistance to fatigue: trained muscles are more efficient at using oxygen and fuel, and can delay lactic acid accumulation, meaning they can sustain high-intensity effort for longer before performance declines. Bone density increases with weight-bearing exercise, making bones stronger and more resistant to injury — a benefit that also protects against conditions such as osteoporosis in later life. Muscular strength increases as hypertrophy and neuromuscular recruitment both improve.

Cardiovascular Adaptations

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are hypertrophy of the heart and a reduction in resting heart rate. The heart grows larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump a greater volume of blood per beat — a greater resting stroke volume. Because resting stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output, resulting in a permanently lower resting heart rate (a long-term adaptation sometimes called bradycardia). While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 bpm, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm.

Capillarisation is another important cardiovascular adaptation. Regular endurance training stimulates the growth of new capillaries in and around the trained muscle groups, increasing capillary density. This improves oxygen delivery to the muscle fibres and speeds up the removal of carbon dioxide and waste products. The overall cardiac output (the maximum amount the heart can pump per minute) also increases with training, as both maximum heart rate is maintained and maximum stroke volume rises. The result is a significantly higher aerobic capacity — the maximum rate at which oxygen can be consumed and used by the muscles during maximal exercise. Finally, rate of recovery improves: a trained athlete’s heart rate returns to resting values more quickly after effort, a sign of cardiovascular efficiency.

A very common exam error is placing a long-term adaptation in the short-term column, or vice versa. “Increased heart rate” is a short-term effect — it happens during a single exercise session and reverses immediately after. “Hypertrophy of the heart” is a long-term effect — it takes months of consistent training to develop. Similarly, “increased breathing rate” is short-term, while “strengthened respiratory muscles” is long-term. When answering exam questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the short term, heart rate increases during the session” vs “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy.”

Respiratory Adaptations

The respiratory muscles — primarily the diaphragm and intercostal muscles — become stronger with regular training, enabling larger tidal volumes and more forceful, efficient breathing. This means trained athletes can ventilate their lungs more effectively at high exercise intensities, maintaining a strong concentration gradient at the alveoli even under heavy muscular demand. Tidal volume and minute ventilation during exercise increase as the respiratory muscles adapt, allowing more air to be moved per breath and per minute.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → hypertrophy of the heart (the heart grows larger) → greater resting stroke volume per beat → lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output. Also: training → capillarisation → improved oxygen delivery to muscle fibres → improved aerobic capacity and resistance to fatigue.

Consider a club cyclist who has been training consistently for two years. In the long term, her heart has undergone hypertrophy, so her stroke volume at rest is around 90 ml compared to the untrained average of 70 ml. Her resting heart rate has dropped from 74 bpm to around 56 bpm. Her muscles have become more capillarised, delivering more oxygen per unit time to her quadriceps and hamstrings. Her respiratory muscles are stronger, and her resistance to fatigue has increased, meaning she can sustain a high power output for longer before lactic acid forces her to ease off. Her aerobic capacity (VO2 max) has improved substantially, and her rate of recovery between efforts has shortened. All of these are the result of systematic, progressive training over months — not a single session.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about effects of exercise is confusing the two timescales. Short-term effects occur during or immediately after exercise — they are temporary. Long-term effects take months or years of consistent training to develop. In “describe” and “explain” questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy, which leads to a lower resting heart rate.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, go beyond listing: connect the adaptation to a named component of fitness and then to a sporting performance benefit. For example: “Capillarisation increases the density of capillaries in the quadriceps, improving oxygen delivery, which improves cardiovascular endurance and allows a county cyclist to sustain a higher pace over a 40 km time trial without fatigue.” The data-handling questions in this topic require you to quote a figure from the table, describe what it shows, and explain the sporting implication — all three steps are needed for full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Short-term effects of exercise include increased muscle temperature, raised heart rate/stroke volume/cardiac output, redistribution of blood flow to working muscles, increased breathing rate and tidal volume, greater oxygen delivery to muscles, and increased lactic acid production during high-intensity effort.
  • Long-term cardiovascular adaptations include hypertrophy of the heart, higher resting stroke volume, lower resting heart rate, improved cardiac output, increased capillarisation and faster rate of recovery.
  • Long-term muscular and respiratory adaptations include hypertrophy of skeletal muscles, improved muscular endurance, greater resistance to fatigue, increased bone density, stronger respiratory muscles and improved aerobic capacity.

lessons.title: Components of Fitness and Fitness Tests
lessons.description: The ten components of fitness, definitions and the standard tests used to measure each.
lessons.content_html:
The Ten Components of Fitness

The specification identifies ten components of fitness. No single sport requires all ten in equal measure, so a key skill is identifying which components are most relevant to a given activity and justifying why. In OCR, component definitions and their standard fitness tests are examined together as a single topic — you must know both the definition of each component and the test used to measure it.

Cardiovascular endurance (also called stamina) is the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to the working muscles during sustained exercise. It is the foundation of performance in long-distance running, cycling, football and rowing. Tests: the Cooper 12-minute run (maximum distance covered in 12 minutes) and the multi-stage fitness test (bleep test — running between two lines 20 m apart in time with a beep that gets progressively faster).

Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle to undergo repeated contractions over a long period without tiring. Important in rowing, cycling and long-distance swimming. Tests: the press-up test (maximum press-ups in one minute) and the sit-up test (maximum sit-ups in one minute).

Speed is the maximum rate at which an individual is able to perform a movement or cover a distance in a period of time. Relevant in sprinting, a winger accelerating past a defender, or a serve in tennis. Test: the 30 m sprint test (time taken to sprint 30 m from a standing start).

Strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert against a resistance. Crucial in scrummaging in rugby, throwing events in athletics and weightlifting. Tests: the grip strength dynamometer test (maximum squeezing force measured in kg) and the 1 Repetition Maximum (1RM) (the heaviest single lift an athlete can perform with correct technique for a given exercise).

Power (also called explosive strength) is the ability to exert maximum force in as short a time as possible — it combines strength and speed. Critical in sprinting, shot-put, plyometric jumps and boxing combinations. Test: the vertical jump test (also called the standing jump test — maximum height of a standing jump, measured in cm).

Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. Crucial in gymnastics, dance, swimming (stroke efficiency) and martial arts. Test: the sit and reach test (reaching forward with straight legs from a seated position, measuring how far beyond the feet the fingers can reach).

Agility is the ability to change body position quickly and accurately while moving. Essential in team sports such as rugby, basketball and hockey where players must dodge opponents and change direction at speed. Test: the Illinois agility test (navigating a timed course with direction changes around cones).

Balance is the ability to retain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support. Can be static (holding a handstand) or dynamic (a gymnast on a balance beam). Important in gymnastics, surfing, skiing and judo. Test: the stork stand test (standing on one leg with the other foot resting against the knee, measuring how long balance can be maintained with eyes closed).

Coordination is the ability to use two or more body parts together smoothly and efficiently. Vital in cricket (eye-hand coordination for batting), tennis and swimming (synchronising arms and legs). Test: the wall throw test (throwing and catching a ball against a wall as many times as possible in 30 seconds, measuring the number of catches).

Reaction time is the time taken to initiate a response to a stimulus. A sprinter reacting to the starting gun, a goalkeeper responding to a shot, and a batsman reading a delivery all depend on a fast reaction time. Test: the ruler drop test (a ruler is dropped without warning and the participant catches it as fast as possible; the distance dropped in cm before it is caught indicates reaction time).

Key Fact

The ten components and their OCR-specified tests: cardiovascular endurance (Cooper 12-min run / multi-stage fitness test); muscular endurance (press-up / sit-up test); speed (30 m sprint); strength (grip dynamometer / 1RM); power (vertical jump); flexibility (sit and reach); agility (Illinois agility test); balance (stork stand); coordination (wall throw); reaction time (ruler drop test). Questions often ask you to select a component, define it AND name its test.

A very common exam error is naming a component without justifying why it matters for the specific sport in the question. Simply writing “cardiovascular endurance is important for football” will not earn full marks. The full answer should name the component, define it, and then give a sport-specific reason: “Cardiovascular endurance — the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to working muscles during sustained exercise — is important for a football midfielder because they must maintain high-intensity running across the full 90 minutes of a match.” Avoid saying “all components are important” — questions are testing your ability to discriminate and prioritise with reasons.

A 100 m sprinter needs: (1) reaction time — to leave the blocks the instant the starter’s pistol fires, reducing the overall race time; (2) power — to accelerate explosively from the blocks during the drive phase; (3) speed — to maintain maximum velocity during the top-speed phase; and (4) muscular endurance — to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10–12 seconds. Cardiovascular endurance is less important than in a marathon because the race duration is too short for the aerobic system to be the limiting factor. Always justify why the component matters for that specific sport — not just list its name.

Key Fact

OCR includes both the Cooper 12-minute run test and the multi-stage fitness test as valid tests for cardiovascular endurance. The Cooper test uses distance (metres) as the measure; the multi-stage test uses a level and shuttle number. Either is acceptable when asked to name a cardiovascular endurance test.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to “define” a component of fitness, you must include the key elements of the definition: for example, cardiovascular endurance requires “heart and lungs” AND “sustained exercise” to earn both marks. On “explain” or “analyse” questions about components, you must name the component, define it briefly AND justify its relevance with a sporting example — three elements are expected. Simply listing components without explanation is a very common error that loses marks. For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, avoid saying “all components are important” — the question is asking you to discriminate, prioritise and justify with reasons. The data-interpretation questions in this topic may include a fabricated fitness test results table — always quote a specific figure, make a comparison, and link to a sporting performance implication.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are ten components of fitness: cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, speed, strength, power, flexibility, agility, balance, coordination and reaction time. Each has a precise definition and a standard OCR-named fitness test.
  • Different sports require different combinations of components; exam questions always require you to name a component, define it and justify its relevance with a specific sporting example.
  • OCR tests include: Cooper 12-minute run and multi-stage fitness test (cardiovascular endurance); press-up and sit-up test (muscular endurance); 30 m sprint (speed); grip dynamometer and 1RM (strength); vertical jump (power); sit and reach (flexibility); Illinois agility test (agility); stork stand (balance); wall throw (coordination); ruler drop test (reaction time).
