lessons.title: Principles of Training and FITT
lessons.description: Specificity, overload, progression, reversibility and the FITT principle applied to training programmes.
lessons.content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session causes the right adaptations without injury or wasted effort. Two frameworks summarise these principles: SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) and FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Together they provide a blueprint for designing any training programme, from a beginner’s fitness plan to an international athlete’s competition preparation.

SPOR: The Four Principles

Specificity — training must be designed to match the specific demands of the sport and the individual. A sprinter must train the fast-twitch muscle fibres and anaerobic energy systems used in a 100 m race; continuous low-intensity jogging would not develop the right adaptations. A swimmer should train in the water to develop sport-specific cardiovascular and muscular endurance rather than only running. If the training is not specific to the sport, the gains will not transfer to performance.

Progressive overload — the body adapts to the demands placed upon it. Once it has adapted, the same training stimulus produces no further improvement. To keep progressing, the training load must be gradually and continuously increased — using the FITT variables. A weight trainer who always lifts the same weight will plateau; they must add weight, more sets or more repetitions to continue building strength. The progression must be gradual: too-rapid increases lead to injury.

Reversibility — fitness adaptations are not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced — due to injury, illness or a long break — the body returns towards its pre-training state. Cardiovascular adaptations (such as a lower resting heart rate and larger stroke volume) reverse relatively quickly, often within a few weeks. Muscle mass is lost more slowly. This principle underlines why consistent, year-round training is more effective than intense bursts followed by long rest periods.

Recovery — sufficient rest must be built into any training programme. Without recovery time, the body cannot repair the microscopic muscle damage caused by training and cannot make the physiological adaptations that lead to improved fitness. Overtraining — training too hard without enough rest — leads to fatigue, declining performance and increased injury risk. Planning rest days or lower-intensity recovery sessions between hard efforts is as important as the training itself.

Key Fact

SPOR: Specificity (match training to sport demands), Progressive Overload (gradually increase load to keep adapting), Overload/reversibility (gains are lost if training stops — see Reversibility), Recovery (adequate rest allows the body to adapt). Note: OCR uses SPOR — Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery — not SPORT. There is no Tedium principle in OCR.

SPOR and FITT are complementary but distinct. SPOR gives the overarching principles — the “why” and “what” of training design (should training be specific? yes; should load progress? yes; must recovery be planned? yes). FITT gives the four variables you can actually manipulate to achieve those principles — the “how.” For example, applying progressive overload (a SPOR principle) is achieved by increasing frequency, intensity or time (all FITT variables). Understanding this relationship is often tested through questions asking you to “apply the FITT principles to achieve progressive overload for a specific athlete.”

FITT: The Four Training Variables

Frequency — how often a person trains per week. A beginner might train twice a week to allow full recovery; an elite endurance athlete may train twice a day. Frequency must be balanced against recovery: too many sessions without rest leads to overtraining and injury, too few limits adaptation.

Intensity — how hard the training is. Intensity can be expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate (for cardiovascular training), a percentage of one rep max (for weight training), or by effort level or speed. The aerobic training zone is 60–80% of maximum heart rate; the anaerobic zone is 80–90%. Choosing the right intensity ensures the correct energy system is stressed.

Time — the duration of a training session or individual exercise bout. A continuous run lasting 30 minutes will primarily stress the aerobic system; interval sprint sessions of 10 seconds each stress the anaerobic system.

Type — the method of training used. Type must align with the principle of specificity: a long-distance runner should use continuous training; a boxer should use circuit training with punching drills and HIIT; a gymnast needing flexibility should include stretching within a structured warm-up and cool-down. Choosing the wrong type of training may improve a general component of fitness without translating to sport-specific performance gains.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard — linked to training zones and heart rate %), Time (how long), Type (which training method). All four can be increased to apply progressive overload. Intensity links directly to training thresholds: aerobic 60–80% max HR; anaerobic 80–90% max HR.

A county-level 400 m freestyle swimmer applies the principles as follows. Specificity: all endurance sessions are in the pool using freestyle technique, not on a running track. Progressive overload: over 12 weeks the swimmer increases weekly distance by 10% and gradually shortens rest intervals between repetitions. Reversibility: during the off-season the swimmer maintains 50% of their training volume with twice-weekly pool sessions so that cardiovascular adaptations are not lost. Recovery: a complete rest day is built in after every two hard training days to allow muscle repair and adaptation. For FITT: frequency moves from 4 to 6 sessions per week over the training block; intensity is set at 70% of max HR for aerobic sets and 85% for higher-intensity sets; time per session increases from 60 to 90 minutes; type rotates between continuous, fartlek and interval training in the pool.

Applying SPOR and FITT Together

The most effective training programmes use both frameworks simultaneously. Specificity determines the training type; progressive overload is achieved by manipulating frequency, intensity and time over weeks and months; reversibility reminds the coach to maintain a training stimulus during breaks; and recovery ensures adequate rest is planned so the body can adapt. When you are asked to “design a training programme” or “evaluate the effectiveness of a training plan,” check whether all four SPOR principles and all four FITT variables are appropriately applied.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sporting example. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progressive overload” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: OCR uses SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) — there is no Tedium principle. Confusing this with other boards’ acronyms is a common error.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SPOR stands for Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility and Recovery — these are the overarching principles that should underpin any training programme. OCR does not include Tedium.
  • FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type — these are the four variables that can be adjusted to implement progressive overload and ensure specificity.
  • SPOR and FITT work together: SPOR explains why changes should be made; FITT explains how to make them in practice.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level distance runner has been following the same 10 km running programme for three months with no improvement in race times. Sporting context maintained throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): identifies progressive overload as the issue; applies two or more FITT variables with some specificity; some reference to sporting context.

Developing (2 marks): identifies that training needs to be harder or more varied; limited use of SPOR/FITT terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant principle mentioned with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. Evaluate how effectively the SPOR principles can be applied to team sport training compared to individual sport training, considering both the benefits and the challenges for a football coach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): evaluates each SPOR principle with a two-sided argument. Specificity: in individual sports (e.g. marathon running) specificity is straightforward — one performer, one event; in football, specificity is harder because different positions require different fitness profiles (a goalkeeper needs different components from a midfielder), so a whole-squad programme may not be fully specific for every player. Progressive overload: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Recovery: in team sport, fixture schedules may not allow ideal recovery between matches, requiring careful management of training load in-season. Evaluates the overall effectiveness, naming specific football examples and contrasting with individual sport examples throughout. Balanced argument sustained.

Secure (5–6 marks): all four SPOR principles covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to football with some comparison to individual sport; generally accurate.

Developing (3–4 marks): at least two SPOR principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.

lessons.title: Methods of Training
lessons.description: Continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT training methods matched to fitness aims.
lessons.content_html:
Why Choose the Right Training Method?

Not all training is created equal. A marathon runner who only does heavy weight training will not improve her aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power he needs off the blocks. Training must be specific to the demands of the sport — this is the principle of specificity in action. Choosing the correct training method is therefore the first and most important decision a coach or athlete makes when designing a programme. OCR identifies seven training methods you need to know: continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a steady pace for a minimum of 20 minutes without any rest breaks. Activities such as running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all commonly used. Because the intensity remains constant and the body has a continuous oxygen supply, continuous training primarily develops cardiovascular endurance. It is well suited to distance runners, rowers and cyclists.

The main advantage is that it is simple, low-cost and easy to monitor — a runner simply keeps going at a steady pace within their aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). A disadvantage is that it can become repetitive and may not replicate the varied demands of team sports, which involve bursts of speed interspersed with periods of lower intensity.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training takes its name from the Swedish for “speed play.” Unlike standard continuous training, fartlek deliberately mixes periods of higher intensity effort with periods of slower recovery running, all without stopping. A footballer might jog steadily for two minutes, then sprint for 30 seconds, then stride at half-pace for a minute, then repeat. Because the performer decides when to change pace, it replicates the unpredictable demands of many team sports.

Key Fact

Fartlek means “speed play” in Swedish. It varies speed and terrain continuously, making it ideal for team-sport athletes whose games combine aerobic and anaerobic demands — such as footballers, rugby players and hockey players.

Interval Training

Interval training uses a planned work:rest ratio — a set period of hard effort followed by a set period of rest or low-intensity recovery. The athlete repeats this pattern for a fixed number of sets. For example, a 400 m track athlete might run 200 m at race pace, rest for 90 seconds, and repeat six times. By controlling the work:rest ratio, the coach can target either aerobic or anaerobic systems: longer work periods with short rests challenge the aerobic system, while very short, maximal sprints with longer rests target the anaerobic system.

Many students assume interval training is always anaerobic because of the repeated high-intensity efforts. In fact, the energy system targeted depends entirely on the work:rest ratio and intensity. A 3-minute effort at 65% maximum heart rate, with 1 minute of walking recovery, repeated five times, is aerobic interval training. Anaerobic interval training requires efforts above 80% of maximum heart rate with longer recovery periods. Always identify the intensity and duration to justify which energy system is being stressed — this is exactly the justification the mark scheme looks for.

HIIT

HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training) is a specific form of interval training where the work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity — typically above 80% of maximum heart rate, within the anaerobic training zone — and rest periods are short. A typical HIIT session might involve 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times. HIIT is time-efficient and produces improvements in both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, making it popular with athletes who are pressed for time.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, performing a specific exercise at each one before moving on to the next. A coach designing a circuit must consider: the space and equipment available, the number of stations, the work:rest ratio at each station, and the type of exercise at each station. The beauty of circuit training is its flexibility — by changing the exercises, the number of stations, the time at each station and the rest periods, the same circuit format can be adapted to develop cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength or power.

For example, a muscular endurance circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, tricep dips and step-ups, each performed for 45 seconds with 15 seconds to move to the next station. To make the same circuit develop strength instead, the coach would add resistance (using dumbbells or weighted vests), reduce the repetitions per station and increase the rest periods.

Weight Training

Weight training uses free weights, machines or bodyweight exercises with added resistance to develop muscular strength, power or muscular endurance. The fitness aim determines the weight and repetitions used. For strength and power, athletes use a high weight (above 70% of one rep max) and a low number of repetitions — approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, athletes use a lower weight (below 70% of one rep max) with a high number of repetitions — approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

Safe practice is non-negotiable: correct lifting technique prevents injury, appropriate weight selection avoids overloading, and a spotter should be present when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press or squat. The back should remain straight during deadlifts and squats to protect the lumbar vertebrae.

Key Fact

Strength/power training: above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps. Muscular endurance training: below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps. The fitness aim determines the weight and rep range.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training develops explosive power. The physiological basis is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle first undergoes a rapid lengthening phase as the athlete lands or prepares, storing elastic energy in the muscle and tendon; this is immediately followed by a powerful shortening contraction as the athlete jumps, bounds or throws. The faster the transition between these two phases, the greater the power output. Exercises include bounding, depth jumping, box jumps and medicine-ball throws. Plyometrics is well suited to sprinters, high jumpers, basketball players and volleyball players — any athlete who needs explosive leg or upper-body power.

Consider a county-level basketball player with a 10-week pre-season. Her coach wants to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular power and agility. An appropriate programme might combine: (1) fartlek training twice a week to mirror the stop-start aerobic and anaerobic demands of a basketball game; (2) plyometric training twice a week (depth jumps and bounding) to improve explosive jumping power for rebounds and lay-ups; (3) HIIT sessions to raise anaerobic threshold and improve the player’s ability to sustain high-intensity efforts late in the fourth quarter. Continuous training alone would be insufficient because it would not develop the anaerobic power the sport demands.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a “6-mark Analyse” question about training methods, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer — for example, only listing advantages of a method without weighing its disadvantages or comparing it to an alternative. Each point should be developed: name the method, describe what it does, link it to a sporting context. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure and anchor every point to a named sport or athlete type. For 2-mark “State Two” questions, make sure your two answers are genuinely different — saying “it improves aerobic fitness” and “it improves cardiovascular endurance” is the same point and will only earn one mark. Remember: OCR lists HIIT as a separate named training method, not just as a category of interval training.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each training method has a primary fitness focus: continuous and fartlek develop cardiovascular endurance; interval and HIIT target aerobic and anaerobic capacity depending on the work:rest ratio; weight training develops strength or muscular endurance depending on the load and rep range; plyometrics develops explosive power.
  • The work:rest ratio is the key variable in interval and circuit training — shorter rests and longer work periods stress the aerobic system, while shorter work periods at maximal intensity with longer rests stress the anaerobic system.
  • Training must always be matched to the demands of the sport (specificity) and the fitness aim of the athlete. Evaluating a method means weighing its advantages and disadvantages in the context of a specific sport and performer.

lessons.title: Warm Up and Cool Down
lessons.description: Components of a warm up, components of a cool down and the physical benefits of each.
lessons.content_html:
Why Warm Up and Cool Down?

Every training session and competitive performance should begin with a structured warm-up and end with a structured cool-down. These are not optional extras — they are physiologically grounded practices that reduce the risk of injury, improve performance quality during the session and accelerate recovery afterwards. OCR is more prescriptive than many boards: it names five specific components of a warm-up and lists eight distinct physical benefits. Knowing both lists precisely is essential.

The Five Components of a Warm-Up

OCR identifies five components in a structured warm-up. They should be delivered in this order, because each builds on the physiological preparation provided by the last.

The first component is a pulse raiser. This involves light aerobic activity — a gentle jog, dynamic movements or easy cycling — that gradually increases the heart rate, raises body temperature and begins redirecting blood flow towards the working muscles through vasodilation. The pace is deliberately modest at the start and builds progressively over several minutes. Starting a session with a flat sprint from cold would risk muscle strains because muscles are stiffer and less pliable at rest.

The second component is mobility exercises. These are controlled rotations and movements of the joints — neck rolls, shoulder circles, hip rotations, ankle circles — that take each joint through its range of motion without the additional challenge of increased load. Mobility work ensures synovial fluid is distributed throughout the joint capsule, making joints more fluid and reducing stiffness before greater demands are placed on them.

The third component is stretching. Dynamic stretching — such as leg swings, hip circles and shoulder rotations — is preferred during a warm-up because it maintains movement and keeps the heart rate elevated. The increased body temperature from the pulse raiser means the muscles are already more pliable, allowing a greater range of movement to be achieved safely.

The fourth component is dynamic movements. These are sport-specific exercises that begin to increase the intensity towards the demands of the activity — for example, lateral shuffles and change-of-direction runs for a netball player, or approach runs for a jumper. Dynamic movements challenge the neuromuscular system with patterns that closely resemble those required in competition, bridging the gap between general preparation and full effort.

The fifth component is skill rehearsal. This involves practising the actual skills of the sport at moderate intensity — a basketball team might include dribbling and shooting drills; a gymnast might rehearse scaled-down versions of her floor routines. Skill rehearsal ensures the neuromuscular system is primed for the precise movement patterns the sport requires and builds confidence before full competitive demands begin.

Key Fact

OCR’s five warm-up components in order: (1) pulse raiser — raises heart rate and body temperature; (2) mobility — loosens joints through their range of motion; (3) stretching — increases muscle pliability and range of movement; (4) dynamic movements — sport-specific exercises at increasing intensity; (5) skill rehearsal — rehearses the precise skills of the sport.

Physical Benefits of Warming Up

OCR lists eight specific physical benefits of a warm-up. Raising body temperature warms the muscles and preparing the body for physical activity so the muscle fibres become more pliable and less susceptible to strain. The elevated body temperature increases the speed at which nerve impulses travel, so the speed of muscle contraction improves — meaning athletes can move and react faster from the very first minutes of exercise.

Blood flow and oxygen delivery to the working muscles increases as cardiac output rises and blood is redirected away from the digestive organs towards the skeletal muscles. This ensures the aerobic energy system is ready to function efficiently from the start. Heart rate increases progressively, preparing the cardiovascular system for the demands ahead rather than shocking it into sudden high demand. Flexibility of muscles and joints improves as the temperature rise makes muscle fibres and surrounding connective tissue more elastic. The pliability of ligaments and tendons also increases with temperature, reducing the likelihood of tears and strains during explosive movements.

Recall from the cardiovascular and respiratory lessons that cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. During a warm-up, both stroke volume and heart rate begin to rise as the body prepares for activity. Blood is redistributed from the digestive organs towards the skeletal muscles through vasodilation in the muscle capillaries. Breathing rate and tidal volume also begin to rise, increasing the oxygen supply reaching the alveoli for gas exchange. A warm-up reinforces this anticipatory cardiovascular and respiratory response and continues the upward physiological response at a controlled pace, reducing the risk of the system being overwhelmed at the start of intense exercise.

The Components of a Cool-Down

After exercise, an immediate stop is physiologically harmful: blood can pool in the lower limbs when muscular contractions no longer pump it back towards the heart, causing dizziness and slowing the removal of waste products. A structured cool-down prevents this. OCR identifies two components: low intensity exercise and stretching.

The first component is low intensity exercise. Moving from a sprint to a jog, then from a jog to a brisk walk, then to a gentle stroll, keeps blood circulating so that lactic acid and carbon dioxide are transported to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal. This gradual decrease also avoids blood pooling in the limbs.

The second component is stretching. After exercise the muscles are warm and pliable — this is the optimal time for static stretching, because the muscle fibres lengthen most easily at elevated temperature. Regular post-exercise stretching helps to maintain and improve flexibility over time. It also reduces the sensation of tightness and stiffness that can set in within hours of a training session.

Key Fact

OCR’s two cool-down components: (1) low intensity exercise (gradual reduction in activity) — maintains blood circulation to remove lactic acid and waste products and prevents blood pooling; (2) stretching — maintains and improves flexibility and reduces post-exercise muscle stiffness.

Physical Benefits of Cooling Down

OCR lists eight specific physical benefits of a cool-down. The body’s transition back to a resting state is managed gradually: heart rate lowers progressively rather than abruptly, and body temperature reduces safely. Blood circulation continues so that oxygen is still supplied to muscles during the recovery phase. Breathing rate gradually reduces as metabolic demand falls. Waste products such as lactic acid are removed more effectively when blood flow is maintained — an athlete who stops abruptly cannot clear waste products as efficiently. The risk of muscle soreness and stiffness is reduced: regular cool-down stretching aids recovery by lengthening muscles that have been held in shortened positions during exercise and reducing the severity of post-exercise soreness.

Lactic acid is produced during anaerobic respiration when the oxygen supply cannot meet the energy demand of the muscles. It accumulates in the muscle and bloodstream during intense exercise, contributing to the burning sensation and fatigue associated with high-intensity effort. During the cool-down, maintaining blood flow allows this lactic acid to be transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose through a process called the Cori cycle. Stretching during the cool-down helps realign muscle fibres and reduce the tight, contracted sensation in muscles that have worked hard. Together, these effects mean the performer can return to quality training sooner.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about warm-up or cool-down, avoid simply listing components. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. For example, rather than writing “the pulse raiser raises heart rate,” develop it: “the pulse raiser gradually raises body temperature, which increases muscle pliability and reduces the risk of muscle strains — particularly important for a gymnast whose movements demand maximum hip and shoulder flexibility from the first routine.” For 2-mark “State Two” questions, ensure your two benefits are genuinely different physiological effects — “raises heart rate” and “increases blood flow” are related but distinct enough to earn two marks, whereas “raises heart rate” and “heart rate goes up” will only earn one. Note: OCR names five warm-up components, not four — mobility and dynamic movements are separate stages.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR’s warm-up has five components in order: pulse raiser (raises heart rate and body temperature), mobility (loosens joints), stretching (increases range of movement), dynamic movements (sport-specific exercises at increasing intensity) and skill rehearsal (rehearses precise sport skills). Together they increase body temperature, blood flow, flexibility and neuromuscular readiness.
  • Physical benefits of warming up include: warming muscles, raising body temperature and heart rate, increasing flexibility of muscles and joints, improving pliability of ligaments and tendons, increasing blood flow and oxygen to muscles, and improving the speed of muscle contraction.
  • A cool-down has two components: low intensity exercise (gradual reduction in intensity to maintain circulation and remove lactic acid) and stretching (aids flexibility and reduces post-exercise stiffness). Benefits include gradually lowering heart rate and temperature, removing waste products, and reducing muscle soreness.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 county-level rugby team has 25 minutes before a regional semi-final. Their coach is planning a structured warm-up. Analyse the importance of each component of an effective warm-up for the rugby players before this match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): all five components identified and each clearly linked to a physiological benefit specific to rugby. Pulse raiser: raises body temperature, increases heart rate and blood flow to muscles needed for explosive sprinting and tackling; mobility: loosens joints, particularly the hips, shoulders and neck which are under significant contact pressure in rugby; stretching: increases flexibility of hamstrings and hip flexors needed for sprinting, and shoulders for tackling and lifting; dynamic movements: includes sprint-and-change-of-direction drills replicating the demands of ruck and maul play; skill rehearsal: includes passing, lineout lifting and scrummaging technique rehearsal to prime neuromuscular pathways specific to rugby decision-making. Uses accurate physiological terminology throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): at least three components described with correct benefits; at least two benefits applied to rugby specifically; generally accurate terminology.

Developing (2 marks): two components identified and described; limited sporting application; one or more physiological effects correctly stated.

Emerging (1 mark): names one component or states one general benefit of warming up without development or application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of including both a warm-up and a cool-down in a training programme for a competitive swimmer who trains six days per week.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): evaluates both warm-up and cool-down with a balanced two-sided argument. Warm-up arguments for: raises body temperature (improves muscle pliability and speed of contraction needed for powerful stroke technique); increases blood flow and oxygen to muscles (supports aerobic energy system from the start of a session); mobilises shoulder and hip joints (high importance in swimming); skill rehearsal of stroke technique primes neuromuscular pathways. Warm-up arguments against/limitation: a swimmer training six days per week may find warm-up time cuts into overall session volume; time pressure in competition warm-up lanes. Cool-down arguments for: removes lactic acid accumulated during intense sprint sets; static stretching maintains shoulder flexibility (high relevance given overuse risk in swimmers); reduces muscle soreness, allowing quality training on consecutive days. Cool-down arguments against/limitation: swimmer fatigue and time pressure may reduce compliance; cool-down in cold pool water may be less effective than on land. Reaches a justified conclusion about relative importance, applying to swimming context throughout.

Secure (5–6 marks): both warm-up and cool-down covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to swimming; generally accurate physiological content.

Developing (3–4 marks): one of warm-up or cool-down covered in more depth; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic statements about one component; little application to swimming; descriptive rather than evaluative.

lessons.title: Preventing Injury in Physical Activity
lessons.description: Strategies that minimise injury risk and the hazards present in different sport and activity settings.
lessons.content_html:
Preventing Injury in Sport and Physical Activity

Injury prevention is not simply a matter of good luck — it is a deliberate, systematic process. Whether an athlete is training in a gym, competing on a grass pitch or swimming in a pool, the environment, equipment, clothing and physical preparation all contribute to the risk of injury. OCR groups injury-prevention strategies under two headings: how the risk of injury can be minimised, and the specific hazards found in each activity setting. Understanding both is essential for the exam.

Minimising the Risk of Injury

Personal protective equipment (PPE) is the first line of defence against contact injuries. In football, shin pads absorb the impact of a tackle to the tibia and fibula, reducing the risk of fractures and lacerations. Cricketers wear a batting helmet, chest guard and leg pads to protect against hard ball impact. Cyclists wear a helmet to protect the cranium in the event of a fall. The key principle is that PPE must be appropriately fitted, in good condition and suited to the specific demands of the sport — a mouthguard designed for rugby cannot be substituted for a simple plastic shield in boxing.

Correct clothing and footwear significantly reduce injury risk. Trainers designed for road running have cushioning and a heel counter that absorbs impact through the tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges on each stride. Football boots with moulded studs provide grip on a grass pitch without locking the foot into the surface — improper footwear such as flat-soled trainers on a wet pitch increases the risk of ankle ligament sprains and falls. Compression garments support the major muscle groups and reduce the risk of muscle strains. Clothing must not restrict movement to the point where it compromises technique, as poor technique itself increases injury risk.

Appropriate level of competition means matching athletes by age, weight, ability and experience. In contact sports such as rugby and boxing, competing against a physically superior opponent increases the forces applied to the body significantly. Weight categories in boxing and wrestling formalise this principle at elite level. For recreational and school sport, it means that a Year-7 student should not be placed in direct contact competition with a Year-11 student, regardless of both students’ technical ability. Mismatched competitions also increase the risk of psychological intimidation, which can cause reckless technique and further injury.

Lifting and carrying equipment safely involves applying correct technique whenever athletes or coaches handle heavy loads — carrying gymnastics apparatus, setting up hurdles, stacking weight plates or moving goal posts. The safe technique requires a straight back, bent knees and a controlled movement using the quadriceps and gluteals to generate force from the legs rather than the lumbar spine. Bending at the waist with a rounded back transfers compressive force directly to the intervertebral discs and lumbar vertebrae, greatly increasing the risk of disc herniation and lower-back injury.

The warm-up and cool-down are powerful injury-prevention tools, not just performance preparation. A warm-up raises muscle temperature, increases the pliability of muscles, tendons and ligaments and prepares the cardiovascular system for the demands ahead — each of these effects directly reduces the risk of soft-tissue injury. A cool-down removes lactic acid via sustained blood flow, reduces the risk of blood pooling in the lower limbs and stretches muscles back towards their resting length, reducing post-exercise stiffness and the chance of injury in subsequent sessions.

Key Fact

OCR’s five injury-prevention strategies: (1) personal protective equipment (e.g. shin pads, helmets); (2) correct clothing and footwear (e.g. sport-specific trainers); (3) appropriate level of competition (matched by age and ability); (4) safe lifting and carrying technique (straight back, bend the knees); (5) use of warm-up and cool-down (raises temperature and removes waste products).

Hazards in Different Activity Settings

OCR requires knowledge of the potential hazards in five named settings. Each setting has specific risks that a performer, coach or official must identify and manage to minimise the chance of injury.

In a sports hall, the most common hazards include slippery floors (from spillages, condensation or inadequate cleaning), equipment left on the floor creating trip hazards, low ceiling height restricting jumping or throwing activities, insufficient space between courts leading to collisions between participants on adjacent pitches, and doors opening into the activity area. Safe practice includes regular floor inspections, storing all equipment on trolleys or in storage areas when not in use, and ensuring adequate clear space around all playing areas.

In a fitness centre, hazards include incorrectly set or poorly maintained weight machines that can trap limbs, free weights left on the floor as trip hazards, wet floors near drinking fountains or water-cooled equipment, cables and resistance bands at head or neck height if set up incorrectly, and the absence of a spotter when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press. Supervision by a qualified instructor is essential in a fitness centre environment to ensure correct equipment use and safe loading.

On a playing field, hazards include uneven ground surface (potholes or ruts that can cause ankle sprains), debris on the pitch (stones, glass or litter), goalposts that are not correctly anchored, extreme weather conditions (frozen or waterlogged ground, lightning risk), poor boundary markings that bring players close to spectator areas, and inadequate footwear for the surface conditions. Pre-match pitch inspections are a standard safety practice in organised sport.

On artificial outdoor areas (synthetic turf, all-weather tracks and courts), hazards include surface abrasion causing skin burns on falls (turf burns), surface hardness increasing impact forces on joints compared to grass, water pooling on non-porous surfaces making them slippery, incorrect footwear (metal studs can catch on artificial fibres and cause ankle injuries), and loose rubber crumb infill that may enter eyes or airways. Appropriate footwear designed specifically for artificial surfaces is essential.

In a swimming pool, the key hazards include slippery pool surrounds causing falls onto hard surfaces, diving into shallow water causing head and cervical spine injuries, overcrowding causing collisions between swimmers, unsafe pool depth for the activity taking place, hazardous pool chemicals if storage protocols are not followed, and hypothermia risk in outdoor pools or cold open-water environments. Lane ropes and clear depth markings are standard safety features that should always be checked before sessions begin.

A common student error is to focus only on PPE and clothing when asked about injury prevention. The OCR specification is explicit that five strategies must be known, and questions often specifically test “other than PPE” scenarios (though note: the spec does not use that exact phrasing — be ready to give any of the five). Similarly, when discussing hazards by setting, students often give vague answers like “wet floor.” For full marks, the answer must name the setting, identify the specific hazard, and explain why it causes injury — for example: “In a swimming pool, slippery pool surrounds increase the risk of falls onto a hard, non-absorbent surface, potentially causing head injuries or fractures.”

A teacher preparing a gymnastics vault session would check: (1) PPE — ensure landing mats are correctly placed and of sufficient thickness to absorb impact forces on landing; (2) clothing — confirm participants are barefoot or wearing grip socks, with no jewellery that could catch on apparatus; (3) appropriate level — group students by ability so novices are not attempting vaults at a height designed for advanced gymnasts; (4) equipment handling — teach students the correct two-person carry technique for moving the vaulting box so no one strains their lumbar spine; (5) warm-up — run a full pulse-raiser and dynamic stretch before any vault attempts so muscle temperature is raised. This five-point checklist maps directly onto OCR’s five injury-prevention strategies and is a useful exam revision structure.

Key Fact

The five OCR activity settings are: sports hall, fitness centre, playing field, artificial outdoor areas, and swimming pool. For each setting, be able to identify at least two specific hazards and explain the injury mechanism (why the hazard causes injury).
lessons.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about injury prevention, the mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sporting application. A common error is listing prevention strategies without explaining how they reduce injury — always link the strategy to the injury mechanism it prevents. For example: “Wearing shin pads in football reduces the risk of tibial fractures and lacerations from direct contact, because the pad absorbs and disperses the impact energy across a larger surface area.” For “Describe” questions about hazards, name the setting, name the specific hazard, and explain why it causes injury. Vague answers such as “the floor could be wet” without naming the setting or injury type will only earn one mark of a possible two or three. For “8-mark Evaluate,” weigh up which strategies are most effective and in which settings — PPE may be critical in contact sport but less relevant in swimming.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Injury risk can be minimised through five OCR strategies: personal protective equipment, correct clothing and footwear, an appropriate level of competition, safe lifting and carrying technique, and use of a warm-up and cool-down. Each strategy targets a different cause of injury.
  • OCR identifies five specific activity settings with distinct hazard profiles: sports hall (slippery floors, trip hazards), fitness centre (unsupervised heavy lifts, loose equipment), playing field (uneven ground, debris, unanchored goalposts), artificial outdoor areas (surface abrasion, inappropriate footwear), swimming pool (slippery surrounds, shallow-water diving).
  • Effective injury prevention combines physical preparation (warm-up), equipment management (PPE, clothing), environmental checks (hazard identification) and matched competition — no single strategy alone is sufficient.

practice_questions.text: Explain how using a warm-up and cool-down before and after exercise can help prevent injury.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: warm-up raises muscle temperature, making muscles more pliable and reducing the risk of strains during explosive movements (1); warm-up increases the pliability of tendons and ligaments, which are more elastic at higher temperatures (1); cool-down maintains blood flow to remove lactic acid and reduce post-exercise muscle stiffness, reducing the risk of injury in subsequent sessions (1); cool-down stretching helps muscles return to their resting length, reducing tightness that could cause compensatory movement patterns and injury in the next session (1).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school PE department is conducting a risk assessment for a swimming gala to be held in the school pool. Analyse the potential hazards present in this setting and how they could be minimised.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies multiple swimming pool hazards with their injury mechanisms and corresponding management strategies, and analyses why each matters in the context of a school event. Slippery pool surrounds: risk of falls onto hard, non-absorbent surface causing head or limb fractures; managed by ensuring non-slip matting around the pool edge and enforcing a no-running rule. Diving into shallow water: risk of cervical spine fractures and serious head injury; managed by enforcing feet-first entry in shallow areas and clearly marking water depth. Overcrowding: risk of collisions during swimming; managed by using lane ropes and staggered heats. Inadequate supervision: a school gala has many young swimmers; managed by having qualified lifeguards positioned at opposite ends of the pool. Chemical hazards: pool chemicals (chlorine, pH adjustment) are hazardous; managed by ensuring storage areas are locked and only accessible to qualified staff. Demonstrates understanding of the link between hazard, injury mechanism and prevention throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): three or more hazards identified with correct injury mechanisms and management strategies; some analysis of why the measures matter in a school context.

Developing (2 marks): two hazards identified correctly; limited analysis; some management strategies.

Emerging (1 mark): one hazard named with minimal development or management strategy.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of personal protective equipment (PPE) and correct clothing and footwear as methods of preventing injury in sport, considering both their benefits and their limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): provides a balanced evaluation of both PPE and clothing/footwear, with benefits and limitations of each applied to named sporting examples. PPE benefits: absorbs or deflects impact forces that would otherwise cause fractures, lacerations or concussions (e.g. a rugby scrum cap reduces the severity of head impacts; shin pads protect the tibia in football). PPE limitations: can only protect the body part it covers; may limit range of movement or create a false sense of security leading to reckless play; must be correctly fitted to be effective — poorly fitting helmets may actually increase injury risk. Clothing/footwear benefits: sport-specific footwear provides appropriate grip and support (e.g. football boots on grass, swimming goggles protecting eyes from chlorine); compression garments support muscles and reduce strain risk. Clothing/footwear limitations: incorrect footwear in one setting may cause injury in another (e.g. metal studs on artificial turf); clothing cannot prevent all impact injuries and may not be a complete substitute for PPE in contact sports. Concludes with a justified assessment of which is more broadly effective or whether both are necessary. Sporting examples used throughout.

Secure (5–6 marks): both strategies covered with some two-sided argument; sporting application present; generally accurate.

Developing (3–4 marks): at least one strategy covered with some benefit and limitation; limited balance; some sporting context.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic statements about PPE or clothing; minimal sporting application; descriptive rather than evaluative.

glossary_terms.definition: Equipment worn to protect the body from impact or injury during sport and physical activity, such as shin pads, helmets, mouthguards and knee pads.
Sportswear and footwear selected to match the demands of the activity, providing appropriate support, protection and freedom of movement.
Ensuring athletes compete against others of similar age, size, experience and ability to reduce the risk of injury from mismatched physical demands.
Using safe biomechanical technique when moving heavy equipment in sport settings: back straight, knees bent, force generated from the legs.
A potential source of harm or injury in a sport or physical activity setting, such as a slippery floor, uneven ground or unsafe equipment.
Skin damage caused by friction between the body and a rough surface such as artificial turf during a fall, resulting in turf burns.
A systematic check of an activity environment to identify potential hazards and the measures needed to reduce the likelihood of injury.
